content: Here is the plan for your animation. Generate makes it.

proposal.title: Gradient descent with two learning rates, side by side
proposal.description: A long, narrow bowl-shaped loss surface has two coloured balls starting from the same point. Each ball follows gradient descent with its own learning rate and leaves a trail. Each step, both balls move together, so you can compare a small rate that creeps slowly to the bottom with a large rate that zig-zags across the narrow valley, or flies off the surface when the rate is too large. Readouts show the step number and each ball's current loss.

input.request: gradient descent with two learning rates

interactions: Press play to let both balls step together, or advance them one step at a time; they stop after 60 steps.
Change either learning rate to compare slow creeping, fast arrival, zig-zagging and divergence.
Pick a different starting point to see how the narrow valley shapes each path.
Turn on the arrows to see the downhill direction (the negative gradient) at each ball; each step moves the ball along its arrow, by the learning rate times the gradient.
Orbit the camera to look at the trails from above or from the side.

proposal.original_request: gradient descent with two learning rates
proposal.prompt: A long, narrow bowl-shaped loss surface has two coloured balls starting from the same point. Each ball follows gradient descent with its own learning rate and leaves a trail. Each step, both balls move together, so you can compare a small rate that creeps slowly to the bottom with a large rate that zig-zags across the narrow valley, or flies off the surface when the rate is too large. Readouts show the step number and each ball's current loss.
requirements: Recommended: experiment. Running both learning rates from the same start on the same surface puts the difference right in front of you: how fast each ball drops, how much it overshoots, and when it diverges. You can set both rates and watch the outcome change.
Interaction: Press play to let both balls step together, or advance them one step at a time; they stop after 60 steps.
Interaction: Change either learning rate to compare slow creeping, fast arrival, zig-zagging and divergence.
Interaction: Pick a different starting point to see how the narrow valley shapes each path.
Interaction: Turn on the arrows to see the downhill direction (the negative gradient) at each ball; each step moves the ball along its arrow, by the learning rate times the gradient.
Interaction: Orbit the camera to look at the trails from above or from the side.
Parameter: Learning rate of ball A (blue), 0.01 to 0.55, default 0.05
Parameter: Learning rate of ball B (orange), 0.01 to 0.55, default 0.45
Parameter: Starting point, one of Far end of the valley, High on the steep side, Corner
Goal: See that the learning rate sets the step size. Too small is slow, a moderate rate converges quickly, and a rate past a limit set by the steepest curvature makes the ball overshoot or diverge.
assumptions: This is an illustration on a made-up bowl-shaped surface, not a real model being trained.
The loss is exactly 0.5·(x² + 4y²): it curves gently along the valley and four times more sharply across it, and its lowest point is at the centre.
Each step is exact plain gradient descent: the new position equals the old position minus the learning rate times the gradient. There is no momentum, noise or schedule.
The surface's height is scaled down for display so the whole bowl stays in view. The loss readouts show the true values.

With this surface, rates below 0.5 shrink the movement across the valley each step. A rate of exactly 0.5 bounces back and forth across it without settling, and rates above 0.5 make that bounce grow until the ball leaves the surface.
limitations: A ball that leaves the drawn area (x from −4 to 4, y from −2 to 2) stops at the edge and is marked as diverged instead of being followed further.
Real loss surfaces have many dimensions and are not shaped like a simple bowl. This one shows how the learning rate behaves in only two directions.
